title: Concept of Health Care Financing
path: Health Care Financing and Insurance Scheme

headings.title: Introduction to Health Care Financing
headings.content: Health care financing is the process through which funds are mobilized, accumulated, and allocated to cover health services for a given population. The primary objective is to ensure that everyone has access to necessary health services—promotion, prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation—without facing financial hardship. When health systems rely heavily on out-of-pocket payments at the point of care, vulnerable households frequently face impoverishment due to unexpected medical bills. A sustainable financing structure decouples the utilization of care from an individual's immediate ability to pay, protecting families from catastrophic health expenditures.

headings.title: Core Functions of Health Care Financing
headings.content:
The framework of health financing rests on three distinct operational pillars:

- **Revenue collection**: The gathering of money from various sources, including general taxation, payroll levies, private insurance premiums, and donor assistance.
- **Pooling**: The accumulation and management of financial resources across a population so that the health risks of the sick are subsidized by the healthy, and the high costs are shared collectively.
- **Purchasing**: The transfer of pooled funds to healthcare providers to deliver specific interventions, ensuring efficiency, quality, and value for money.

headings.title: Sources of Health Care Funds
headings.content: Health systems draw their operational capital from multiple streams. **General government revenue** comes from national and sub-national taxes, forming the bedrock of public health budgets. **Social health insurance** relies on mandatory payroll contributions tied to employment status. **Private health insurance** involves voluntary commercial premiums purchased by individuals or corporate employers. **Out-of-pocket spending** represents direct payments made by patients at the point of service delivery. Finally, **external aid and donor funding** stem from international agencies and foreign governments, supporting specific disease control programs in developing nations.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Risk Pooling and Purchasing
headings.content: Risk pooling is the heart of financial protection. Without it, health care acts like a commercial market where individuals pay strictly for what they consume. Effective pooling cross-subsidizes the healthy with the sick and the rich with the poor. Strategic purchasing takes this a step further. Instead of blindly reimbursing providers for every single service rendered—which encourages over-servicing—purchasers use data to buy cost-effective, high-priority interventions. Strategic purchasers actively contract providers based on quality standards and performance metrics.

headings.title: Overview of Health Insurance Systems in Nigeria
headings.content: Nigeria operates a pluralistic health financing landscape. The formal framework is anchored by the **National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)**, which succeeded the older NHIS to mandate health coverage and drive the realization of universal access. Despite this, coverage remains heavily skewed. The formal sector—such as civil servants and organized private employees—experiences higher enrollment through contributory schemes. Conversely, the vast informal sector, representing the majority of the population, largely depends on out-of-pocket spending. State-level health insurance agencies (SHIAs) have also emerged to capture informal workers and vulnerable groups through subsidized state-level programs.

headings.title: Challenges of Health Care Financing in Developing Countries
headings.content: Developing nations face structural barriers that hinder effective health financing. A massive **informal economy** makes payroll tax collection nearly impossible for social insurance schemes. Governments frequently allocate sub-optimal budgetary percentages to health, falling far short of international agreements like the Abuja Declaration. Widespread **poverty** limits the capacity of citizens to pay voluntary premiums. Additionally, heavy dependence on external donor funding creates vulnerability when international priorities shift, while institutional corruption and inefficient resource allocation drain available capital.

headings.title: Strategies for Achieving Universal Health Coverage
headings.content: Universal Health Coverage (UHC) means all people receive the quality health services they need without financial ruin. Achieving this requires deliberate policy shifts. Governments must increase domestic resource mobilization by expanding tax bases and sealing leakages. Pre-payment mechanisms—such as taxes and social insurance—must replace out-of-pocket spending. Equity funds should be established to subsidize premiums for indigents, pregnant women, and children under five. Finally, health service delivery must be restructured to strengthen primary health care as the most cost-effective entry point.

headings.title: The Role of Nurses in Health Care Financing and Resource Allocation
headings.content: Nurses are active participants in the economic life of a health facility, far beyond direct bedside care. As frontline clinical managers, they directly influence resource allocation by preventing waste, managing consumable inventories carefully, and reducing hospital-acquired complications that prolong length of stay. Furthermore, nurse leaders advocate for resource distribution that prioritizes underfunded primary care units. Understanding health financing allows nurses to engage in policy discussions, participate in health insurance accreditation processes, and educate patients on utilizing available prepayment schemes.
